title: Slow Water
passage:
Ask anyone who has argued for the return of beavers to a British headwater what the animals are for, and the answer comes back in cubic metres. A dam ponds water; a chain of dams ponds a great deal of it; and water sitting in a pond is water not running towards the town at the bottom of the valley. The arithmetic is easy to carry in the head, and it has done more for the case than any argument about willow ever did. Storage is the figure quoted at consultations, printed on posters and totted up in hectare-metres by volunteers with tape measures. What it assumes is that a flood peak is made of volume. It is made of timing.

That assumption has now been put to a catchment. Over nine years the hydrologist Anneke Sorrel and her group followed eleven headwater sub-catchments of the Ferrow into which beavers had returned at different dates, keeping the rainfall record and the gauging method common to all of them and letting the dams accumulate as the colonies saw fit. On the figure the leaflets quote, the result was everything the campaigners had promised. Dam count tracked storage almost exactly, storage rose year on year, and in the ordinary winter storms — the ones that come six or seven times a winter — the peak that reached the gauge at Millstake was lower than before the beavers, and it arrived later. That held in all eleven sub-catchments, the steep peaty ones and the gentle grazed ones alike.

Then Sorrel's group stopped counting ordinary storms and looked at the rare ones. A defence at the bottom of a valley is not built for the rain that comes six times a season but for the storm that comes once in a working life, and it was in those that stored volume stopped predicting anything. Across the fourteen largest events in the record, the drop in peak height at Millstake bore almost no relation to how much water the dams upstream could hold. What it tracked instead was where those dams were. Where colonies had spread across several tributaries, the peak was blunted more often than not; where a similar volume of pond sat in one long chain on a single tributary, it was not, and in two of the fourteen the gauge read a little higher than it had in the pre-beaver years. Sorrel will not push the explanation far. The tributaries of the Ferrow are of very unequal length, she points out, and water entering the highest of them takes the better part of a day longer to reach Millstake than water entering the lowest; a chain of ponds on one tributary fills, spills and empties on a single schedule. There is a ceiling on it in any case. Once the rain has run long enough for every pond in a sub-catchment to fill — about forty hours in the Ferrow — the freeboard is gone, and the water is passed down much as it would have been before the animals came back.

This is not how the argument is usually conducted. Douglas Traer, who has campaigned for a decade to get beavers into the next valley, has no patience for qualifications. "Every dam is a flood defence, and every pond is money the council does not have to spend on concrete," he told me. "Engineers have had two centuries and a great deal of public money, and the town still floods. Put the animals back and stand out of the way." Sorrel is more careful. Where the dams end up can be nudged, she says, by fencing, by planting and by leaving some tributaries to themselves — but the gain against the largest storms is modest, and the window in which it works is narrower than any leaflet admits.

Read whole, the Ferrow record is more divided than either side's leaflet. It does not make the animals decorative: in the ordinary storms the ponds do the obvious work, and the reduction is real enough for the people at the bottom of the valley to feel it in a wet January. What it unsettles is the figure the argument has been conducted in. Volume is easy to measure, easy to add up and easy to put on a poster, and when the water is high it predicts very little. How the dams are spread across a catchment's tributaries is awkward to measure and predicts a good deal. On the Ferrow, at least, what the beavers did with a flood was not so much hold it back as take it apart.
— Peter Mallow

catchment = the whole area of land whose rainfall drains into one river
freeboard = the depth of empty pond left above the water line before it spills

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: That the volunteers who tot up pond storage in hectare-metres are measuring the ponds far too crudely for their totals to be trusted.
That bringing beavers back to a river restores a wetland whose real value the arithmetic of flood storage was never going to capture.
That beaver ponds do lower ordinary flood peaks, but in the rarest storms what counts is the spread of the dams, not their volume.
That a chain of dams along a single tributary leaves the valley below worse off in a big storm than having no beavers at all.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text gist), edge position 1. WHY-KEY (C): the arc is phenomenon → evidence → complication → verdict. The received figure is storage ('Storage is the figure quoted at consultations, printed on posters and totted up in hectare-metres'); the evidence paragraph confirms it on that figure ('in the ordinary winter storms … the peak that reached the gauge at Millstake was lower than before the beavers, and it arrived later'); the complication overturns it for the rare events ('Across the fourteen largest events in the record, the drop in peak height at Millstake bore almost no relation to how much water the dams upstream could hold. What it tracked instead was where those dams were'); and the verdict names the swap explicitly ('Volume … when the water is high it predicts very little. How the dams are spread across a catchment's tributaries is awkward to measure and predicts a good deal'). C paraphrases exactly that two-part shape and keeps both scopes intact. WHY-NOT-A (trap: scope_error / detail-as-main, distorted): the volunteers with tape measures are a single scene-setting clause in paragraph 1, and the text never says their measurements are crude or untrustworthy — its complaint is that the quantity itself predicts little when the water is high, which is a different objection. A blind reader who has caught the word 'arithmetic' finds this live, but it promotes a vivid detail and misstates the flaw. WHY-NOT-B (trap: outside_knowledge): habitat and wetland value is the most familiar real-world case for beaver reintroduction, so a passage-blind reader will consider it, but this text argues entirely inside flood hydrology and never mentions habitat, species or wetland value. WHY-NOT-D (trap: quantifier_upgrade of a sub-point): the passage reports that where a similar volume sat in one long chain the peak was not blunted, and that 'in two of the fourteen the gauge read a little higher than it had in the pre-beaver years' — two events out of fourteen, and only a little. D upgrades that to a general rule about what a chain does to a valley, and promotes a sub-finding to the thesis.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the ordinary winter storms in the Ferrow?

options.text: The peak reaching the gauge was lower and later than before the beavers, in all eleven sub-catchments alike.
The peak fell in most of the sub-catchments, though the steep peaty ones showed no measurable change.
In these storms the drop in peak height had almost nothing to do with the volume the dams could hold.
Sorrel's team drew the ponds down ahead of each forecast storm so that they would have room for the rainfall.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 2. WHY-KEY (A): 'in the ordinary winter storms — the ones that come six or seven times a winter — the peak that reached the gauge at Millstake was lower than before the beavers, and it arrived later. That held in all eleven sub-catchments, the steep peaty ones and the gentle grazed ones alike.' A recasts both halves — the direction of the change and its universality across the sub-catchments — without reusing the sentence. Note the deliberate hedge inversion: the key is the confident, absolute claim here, because the passage licenses it. WHY-NOT-B (trap: quantifier_downgrade with a scope flaw): 'most … though the steep peaty ones showed no measurable change' contradicts 'all eleven sub-catchments, the steep peaty ones and the gentle grazed ones alike'. It is the more cautious-sounding option, which is exactly why a test-wise solver reaching for the hedged answer is punished. WHY-NOT-C (trap: wrong_location): the claim is true of the fourteen largest events in paragraph 3, not of the ordinary winter storms this stem asks about; the opening words 'In these storms' relocate it and make it false. WHY-NOT-D (trap: outside_knowledge): drawing reservoirs down before a forecast storm is standard practice on engineered catchments and sounds like sensible method, but nothing in the text says the ponds were managed at all — Sorrel's group kept the method common across the sub-catchments while 'letting the dams accumulate as the colonies saw fit'.

questions.prompt: What are we told about long spells of rain in the Ferrow catchment?

options.text: Water entering the highest tributaries reaches the gauge sooner than water that enters the tributaries lower down.
The dams give way under the weight of the water and let the whole store down at once.
The beavers abandon the highest ponds and the colony works its way down towards the main river.
Once every pond has filled the catchment passes the water on much as it did before the beavers.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in the closing sentences of paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (D): 'Once the rain has run long enough for every pond in a sub-catchment to fill — about forty hours in the Ferrow — the freeboard is gone, and the water is passed down much as it would have been before the animals came back.' D paraphrases the ceiling: full ponds, no freeboard, pre-beaver routing. WHY-NOT-A (trap: reversed detail): the passage says the opposite — 'water entering the highest of them takes the better part of a day longer to reach Millstake than water entering the lowest'. The option recycles the travel-time material and inverts its direction, which a skimmer who remembers only that the tributaries differ in length will accept. WHY-NOT-B (trap: outside_knowledge / plausible mechanism never stated): dam failure under load is the obvious thing a reader expects to happen in prolonged rain, and it would explain a lost benefit; the passage instead describes ponds that 'fill, spill and empty' and freeboard that runs out, never a breach. WHY-NOT-C (trap: outside_knowledge): a natural-history claim about colony behaviour that sounds entirely plausible for beavers under flood, but the text says nothing about where the animals go — it tracks water, not lodges.

questions.prompt: Sorrel points out that the Ferrow's tributaries are of very unequal length. What does the text suggest follows from this?

options.text: The longest tributaries deliver most of a flood, so the dams that sit on them do most of the useful work.
Water from different tributaries needs different amounts of time to arrive, so spread-out dams keep the peaks from coinciding.
A chain of dams on one tributary can hold appreciably more water than the same dams spread across several.
Water from the higher tributaries arrives too late to be counted in the peak that the gauge records.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 3. The passage supplies the premise without drawing the conclusion: 'The tributaries of the Ferrow are of very unequal length, she points out, and water entering the highest of them takes the better part of a day longer to reach Millstake than water entering the lowest; a chain of ponds on one tributary fills, spills and empties on a single schedule.' WHY-KEY (B): unequal length means unequal travel times, and dams held on separate tributaries therefore release on separate clocks, so the tributary contributions cross the gauge apart rather than together — which is what flattens a peak, and why 'a chain of ponds on one tributary fills, spills and empties on a single schedule' does not. The text states the travel-time premise and the single-schedule observation but never joins them; that join is the single inch it leaves the reader to walk. WHY-NOT-A (trap: too_far / outside_knowledge): plausible catchment reasoning — long tributary, more land, more water — and it uses the stem's own premise, but the passage never ranks tributaries by how much flood they deliver, only by how long their water takes to arrive. WHY-NOT-C (trap: surface_word_match on the storage idea, and contradicted): this is the volume intuition the whole passage is written against, and it is defeated by a phrase a careful reader can point to — 'where a similar volume of pond sat in one long chain on a single tributary'. Volume was matched; distribution was the variable. WHY-NOT-D (trap: too_literal_or_too_far — one step too far): it takes the true premise (water from the highest tributaries arrives much later) and adds an unsupported consequence, that late water falls outside the recorded peak. The text says nothing of the sort; late arrival is what spreads the flood out, not what hides it from the gauge.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to Traer's case for beavers?

options.text: He accepts Traer's arithmetic: every pond is money the council no longer has to spend on concrete, and the engineers have had their turn.
He takes Sorrel's qualifications seriously but concludes that the Ferrow record, read whole, broadly bears out what the leaflets claim.
He grants that the animals buy something real, while holding that the gain is too narrow to stand in for engineered defences.
He finds the campaign sentimental and the flood benefit too slight to be worth the trouble of measuring.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / attitude), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (C): the writer concedes the substance — 'It does not make the animals decorative: in the ordinary storms the ponds do the obvious work, and the reduction is real enough for the people at the bottom of the valley to feel it in a wet January' — while the complication and Sorrel's summary bound it: 'the gain against the largest storms is modest, and the window in which it works is narrower than any leaflet admits'. Traer's case is that ponds substitute for concrete ('money the council does not have to spend on concrete'); the writer's verdict grants the benefit and denies the substitution. WHY-NOT-A (trap: role_or_attribution_swap — the TYPE-005 signature): this is Traer's own position, quoted, offered as the writer's. The passage frames it as the thing that is 'not how the argument is usually conducted' and immediately answers it with Sorrel's caution. WHY-NOT-B (trap: direction reversal, hedged in form): deliberately built to be as measured-sounding as the key, so that 'pick the cautious option' decides nothing. It fails on direction: the verdict says the leaflets' figure 'predicts very little' when the water is high, which is not a broad vindication. WHY-NOT-D (trap: polarity overshoot): dismissiveness overshoots the hedged verdict and is directly contradicted by 'It does not make the animals decorative' and by the reduction being 'real enough … to feel it in a wet January'.
